title: Container Image Scanning
summary: Container image scanning inspects the layers, package manifests and configuration of a container image to find known-vulnerable software components, embedded secrets, malware and risky settings before the image is deployed or while it sits in a registry. Scanners enumerate installed packages with their versions and match them against vulnerability data keyed by package name, version and distribution, and they also read image metadata such as the base image, exposed ports, user and build history. Findings need triage, because a base image often carries packages that the running process never invokes and cannot reach, so reachability and severity matter more than raw counts. The technique is applied in three places: the build pipeline, where the fix belongs in the Dockerfile or dependency file, the registry, where images are re-evaluated as new vulnerability data arrives, and admission control, where a policy refuses to run an image that breaches a threshold. The mistake is scanning only at the end of the pipeline and forgetting that an unchanged image becomes riskier every day.

beginner.definition: Container image scanning means checking a container image for software with known security problems. An image is like a sealed box that holds an application and everything it needs. The scanner reads the list of contents and compares it with a list of known weak versions. It then reports what it found, so you can update or remove it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Container images often include old libraries that nobody remembers adding. Attackers look for those same known weak versions when they break into a cluster. Scanning finds them before the image reaches production. It also catches secrets that were copied into the image by mistake. Without scanning, one old flaw in a shared base image can quietly affect hundreds of containers.
howItWorks: The scanner reads the image layers and lists every installed software package.
It compares each name and version with a database of known issues.
It also looks for private keys, passwords and risky settings inside the image.
Results come back as a list with a severity and a suggested fix.
The team updates the base image or the dependency, then builds again.
A policy in the pipeline or cluster can block an image that fails.
beginner.example: Think of a delivery company that checks every parcel before loading the van. Workers open the box, read the list of contents and look for anything banned, such as a leaking battery. If they find something, the parcel goes back to the sender instead of onto the road. A container image scanner does that check for software. The best moment to catch the problem is at the sender, well before the parcel travels.
takeaways: Scan early in the build, so the fix lands in the image recipe, not in a report.
Triage findings, because not every vulnerable package can actually be reached.
Vulnerability data changes daily, so scan again even when the image does not.

objectives: Explain what container image scanning looks for and where in the lifecycle it runs.
Describe how installed packages are matched against known vulnerability data.
Explain why findings must be triaged for reachability, severity and exploitability.
Describe how a registry or admission policy blocks an image that fails a threshold.
Explain why an unchanged image can become riskier over time.
